newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SA WEEK AHEAD - LAST GASP FOR CREDIT BOOM, GDP FLAGS.
newsitem.headline: SA WEEK AHEAD - LAST GASP FOR CREDIT BOOM, GDP FLAGS.

text.p: South African private credit extension will have ballooned again in October but this may be the last gasp of a consumer spending splurge funded on borrowed money, economists said.
The consensus forecast of 13 economists polled by Reuters was that private sector credit extension expanded 18.1 percent year-on-year in October, with the forecast range 17.7 to 18.6.
That compares with a preliminary September figure of 17.94 percent, but this is expected to be revised upwards when the latest data is released on Friday.
M3 money supply growth is forecast at 15.1 percent -- with a range 14.1 to 15.5 percent -- after September's 14.45 percent.

More bad money supply figures are unlikely to surprise South Africa's jaundiced markets, especially since Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals gave excess credit growth as a key reason for hiking the Bank rate one point to 17 percent last week.

Economists said credit demand continued to be driven by pre-emptive buying ahead of expected price rises caused by the rand's fall -- a fact highlighted by a leap in October new car sales to the highest level in more than a decade.
But the annual credit growth figure was also being kept high by last year's relatively low comparative base, and most analysts believe the credit boom has now peaked.
"I think this figure is going to be the high point. November may be around 18 percent but the trend from here will be down," said Herman van Papendorp of SMK Securities.
Carole Mason, group economist at Investec Bank, agreed: "If we are not at the peak now, we must be very, very close to it."
This week's interest rate hike, which took the prime lending rate up to 20.25 percent -- or over 11 percent in real terms -- will squeeze borrowing out of the system sooner or later.

"I'm fairly confident we are going to see a dramatic decline next year...I wouldn't be surprised if we see total money supply (growth) of around eight percent towards the end of next year," said Johan Roussouw of stockbroker Huysamer Stals.

Punishing real interest rates may finally allow Stals to defeat his credit extension bogey, even permitting a rate cut within six months or so. But the price will be high on an already flagging economy.
Third quarter gross domestic product (GDP) figures, due on Thursday, are expected to show growth slowing sharply, if the rampant agricultural sector is stripped out.
Even with agriculture, the consensus forecast of economists is for quarter-on-quarter seasonally-adjusted and annualised growth of 2.5 percent, against 3.5 in the second quarter.

The forecast range was wide at 1.0 to 3.5 percent, with economists differing on how much of this year's bumper maize crop would be included in the third quarter figures and how much had already been included in the previous period.
Kevin Lings of Nedcor expects the bulk of the crop to register in the third quarter, boosting agriculture by 60 percent.
"Agriculture is the big number. If you take out agriculture you are looking at around 0.7 percent," he said.

Manufacturing, accounting for 25 percent of GDP, is expected to show little if any growth in the third quarter while mining will be weighed down by a weak performance by gold, partly offset by coal's stronger showing.
Looking ahead, economists see a bleak start to 1997, although the depreciation in the rand should finally start to kick in and help the export sector of manufacturiing in the second half.
Lings said the latest rate hike had caused his bank to revise down its full-year 1997 growth forecast to just 2.0 percent from 2.2 percent forecast previously.

Also due out next week, from Monday, are October trade figures, originally expected this week. The consensus forecast is for a 900 million rand surplus compared with a 666.7 million rand surplus in September.
